title: Index Funds Pay 4% More on Rebalancing: Passive Investing Is More Than Just Indexing
dek: David Booth breaks down the difference between index funds and passive investing: index rebalancing pushes stock prices up 4%, true passivity is scientific pricing plus fine execution; the 10% annual return over a century is driven by humanity's desire to improve.
why: High information density, with both a mechanism breakdown of the hidden costs of index funds and the execution philosophy of a 50-year veteran, suitable for those who want to understand how 'scientific investing' actually lands.
who: Passive fund practitioners, financial advisors, individual investors skeptical of index fund efficiency, and quant novices who want to know how 'scientific investing' is implemented.
skip: The opening shoe store anecdote and the closing art collection passage can be fast-forwarded without missing the main thread.

points.h: Not selling ill-fitting shoes matters more than closing the deal
points.body: David Booth worked as a commission-based salesman during high school and college. He found that although he wanted to make the sale, he wanted to feel good about himself when he went home at night, so he never sold shoes that didn't fit. This experience has nothing to do with investment philosophy, but it shaped Dimensional's business philosophy: be honest with clients, and if there's no suitable product, say so directly. He admits to regrettable sales early on, but decided not to repeat them. In the long run, scientifically grounded practices plus good arguments naturally earn trust.

points.h: Outsiders don't get taken advantage of and dare to challenge assumptions
points.body: David's parents lived through the Great Depression and always considered themselves outsiders to the capital markets, afraid of being taken advantage of by insiders, so they never invested. But he points out that the financial science of the 60s and 70s boiled down to two points: long-term returns on stocks and bonds meet expectations, and professional fund managers underperform the market after fees. These two points made it clear to outsiders that public markets are fair to everyone. The outsider mindset also brings a benefit: a willingness to challenge assumptions. The scholars who changed finance back then were also outsiders because they had data, making conclusions that Wall Street hated hard to refute.

points.h: Index funds are a product of marketing genius, not scientific conclusion
points.body: David emphasizes distinguishing passive management from index funds. He notes that the most important change in the financial industry over the past century is the shift to passive management, but index funds are a product of marketing genius, not what scientists would conclude. Scientists wouldn't impose a 'must track an index' constraint on a portfolio because constraints have an economic cost. The index itself is a human-managed portfolio; for example, the S&P 500 is not strictly the top 500 companies, and inclusions and exclusions involve judgment. Dimensional considers itself passive, not indexed.

points.h: The cost of trading at the closing price is paying 4% more
points.body: When a stock is added to the S&P 500, index funds must buy at the closing price on that day. David says you can ask a broker to guarantee execution at the closing price, but the cost is 'willing to pay any price.' When all S&P 500 managers do this simultaneously, they push the stock price up by an average of 4% above fair value. It's like a three-card monte game: investors think they're not paying transaction costs, but the 4% premium reverts the next day. This is the hidden cost of index funds, and it's why passive managers can do better.

points.h: Investors in 1971 had it an order of magnitude worse than today
points.body: Asked whether he'd rather be an investor in 1971 or today, David unhesitatingly chose today. In 1971, management fees were as high as 1-2% per year, and NYSE-set commission rates were an order of magnitude higher than today, even 10-20 times higher; institutions, to absorb high commissions, spawned the 'soft dollar' industry, similar to paying high ticket prices for double miles. Custody costs were also high, with some banks still keeping handwritten ledgers. In contrast, today's costs and transparency give ordinary investors a much fairer deal.

points.h: Research is a public good; the gap is only in execution
points.body: David points out that financial science has become public knowledge, especially because Fama and French insisted on making their research public, but competitors' new research may not be peer-reviewed. He believes that with thousands of professors mining the same data for decades, it's unlikely there will be a disruptive new result. The real difference lies in implementation: Myron Scholes said, 'Ideas are cheap; execution is what matters.' Execution is not just placing orders; it includes the engineering of portfolio construction. Ken French treats execution as engineering; always buying at the ask and selling at the bid in trading accumulates losses over time, which is why Dimensional developed fine trading techniques.

points.h: 10% annual return isn't magic; it's people refusing to sit still
points.body: David explains why stocks have returned about 10% annually over the long term: it's not magic, but humanity's instinct to improve. At the start of the pandemic, U.S. stocks fell about 30%, and he told clients he didn't know what would happen, but he believed companies wouldn't sit still—they would innovate, shut down, pivot—and the recession lasted only one quarter. This is also why you should hold a market portfolio rather than individual stocks—individual stocks can go to zero, but the market won't. Holding the market portfolio is a bet on the overall economy and the human creativity within it.

points.h: No matter how hot private markets get, they're not worth leaving your comfort zone
points.body: Pressed on his view of private markets, David said bluntly, 'I'm not tempted.' He likes the transparency of public markets: listed companies must disclose a lot of information, there are countless price discoveries every day, liquidity is always available, and tax reporting is timely. He says he already has a strategy he considers fair and doesn't want to leave his comfort zone for something unfamiliar. He even says that if he were an advisor, he'd allow clients to play with 10% of their money in individual stocks, private equity, or venture capital, but the other 90% must follow a rigorous process.
